title: Rajma Nutrition Facts: Protein, Fibre, and the Real Rajma Chawal Calorie Count
meta_description: 100g cooked rajma has about 9g protein, 6.4g fibre, and a low glycaemic index of roughly 25–29. Full macro breakdown, plus what a real bowl of rajma chawal actually costs you in calories.
meta_keywords: rajma protein nutrition facts, rajma nutrition per 100g, rajma chawal calories, rajma glycaemic index, kidney beans protein India
quick_answer: 100g of cooked rajma (kidney beans) contains about 8.5–9g protein, 127 kcal, 22–23g carbohydrate, and 6.4g fibre. It has a low glycaemic index — roughly 25–29 — meaning it digests slowly and doesn't spike blood sugar. A typical bowl of rajma chawal (1 cup rajma curry + 1 cup rice) works out to roughly 13–15g protein and 400–440 kcal, most of which comes from the rice and cooking oil rather than the beans themselves.

faq.question: How much protein is in 100g of cooked rajma?
faq.answer: About 8.5–9g protein per 100g of plain boiled rajma (kidney beans), along with 127 kcal, 22–23g carbohydrate, and 6.4g fibre. Dry, uncooked rajma is much more protein-dense at roughly 22–24g protein per 100g, but it triples in weight during soaking and cooking, which dilutes the numbers per 100g of the cooked, edible portion.

faq.question: Is rajma good for weight loss?
faq.answer: Yes, in reasonable portions. Rajma combines protein, high fibre (6.4g per 100g cooked), and a low glycaemic index, which together support satiety and steady blood sugar — all favourable for weight management. The calorie cost of a typical meal comes mostly from the oil in the curry and the rice served alongside it, not from the rajma itself.

faq.question: Is rajma chawal a complete protein meal?
faq.answer: Close to it. Rajma, like most legumes, is low in the amino acid methionine but rich in lysine; rice is the reverse — low in lysine, adequate in methionine. Eating them together, as rajma chawal does by default, provides a fuller amino acid profile than either food alone — a classic legume-plus-grain combination that shows up across Indian, and global, home cooking for exactly this reason.

intro: Rajma chawal is comfort food first and a protein source second in most people's minds, which undersells what's actually in the bowl. Kidney beans are one of the more fibre-dense, slow-digesting legumes in the everyday Indian kitchen, and the protein numbers hold up reasonably well too — the part that actually needs scrutiny is what happens once the beans become a curry sitting next to a plate of rice. Here is the full breakdown, and an honest accounting of what a real bowl costs you.

sections.heading: The number: rajma macros per 100g cooked
sections.body:
100g of plain boiled rajma (kidney beans, no oil or masala) contains approximately:

• Protein: 8.5–9g
• Calories: 127 kcal
• Carbohydrate: 22–23g
• Fibre: 6.4g
• Fat: 0.5g

For comparison, dry uncooked rajma is far more concentrated — roughly 22–24g protein per 100g — but soaking and boiling roughly triples the weight as the beans absorb water, so the per-100g numbers drop once you're measuring the cooked, edible portion. When a recipe or nutrition label says "100g rajma," always check whether that's dry weight or cooked weight; the difference changes the protein number by nearly 3x.

sections.heading: Fibre and glycaemic index: why rajma digests slowly
sections.body:
At 6.4g fibre per 100g cooked, rajma is one of the higher-fibre foods in a typical Indian thali — more than most cooked dals, and well above rice or roti. That fibre, combined with a low glycaemic index of roughly 25–29, is what gives rajma its reputation as a slow, steady-release carbohydrate source rather than a blood-sugar spike.

In practical terms: the combination of protein, fibre, and low GI means rajma keeps you full longer per calorie than most other starch-adjacent foods on an Indian plate, including plain rice or potato-based dishes.

sections.heading: Rajma vs other common legumes: protein comparison
sections.body:
Per 100g cooked, here's how rajma stacks up against other legumes common in Indian cooking:

• Rajma (kidney beans): 8.5–9g protein, 127 kcal, 6.4g fibre
• Masoor dal (red lentils): 9g protein, 116 kcal, 7.9g fibre
• Chana (chickpeas): 8.9g protein, 164 kcal, 7.6g fibre
• Moong dal (split): 7g protein, 105 kcal, 7.6g fibre

The differences between these are minor — all cooked legumes land in a similar 7–9g protein per 100g range. What actually separates them for a weight-conscious diet is less about protein and more about how they're traditionally cooked: rajma and chana are usually simmered in a heavier oil-based gravy, while masoor and moong are more often made as a thinner, lighter-oil dal.

sections.heading: What the curry adds: rajma vs rajma masala
sections.body:
Plain boiled rajma at 127 kcal per 100g is lean. Turn it into rajma masala — onion-tomato gravy, 1–2 tablespoons of oil or ghee per serving, plus butter or cream in restaurant versions — and a typical 1-cup serving (about 200g of curry, roughly 100–120g beans plus gravy) rises to approximately:

• Protein: 9–10g
• Calories: 180–220 kcal
• Fat: 8–12g

As with most Indian legume curries, the protein barely moves — it's almost entirely from the beans — while the calorie increase comes from the oil the gravy is built on. A home-style rajma made with 1 teaspoon of oil per serving stays much closer to the plain-boiled numbers than a restaurant version finished with butter.

sections.heading: The rajma chawal reality check
sections.body:
Here is the full plate, not just the curry. A standard home serving of rajma chawal — 1 cup rajma curry (roughly 200g) plus 1 cup cooked white rice (roughly 158g) — works out to approximately:

• Protein: 13–15g
• Calories: 400–440 kcal
• Carbohydrate: 65–70g
• Fibre: 7–9g

The rice contributes roughly half the calories and most of the carbohydrate, with about 4g of that protein. This isn't a criticism of rajma chawal as a meal — it's a genuinely well-rounded plate with decent protein, strong fibre, and a low-GI profile overall. It just isn't a high-protein meal by itself the way, say, a dal-paneer combination would be. Pairing it with a side of curd (roughly 11g protein per cup) is a simple way to push the full meal past 24–26g protein without changing the core dish.

key_takeaways: 100g cooked rajma = 8.5–9g protein, 127 kcal, 6.4g fibre — dry rajma is far more protein-dense (22–24g/100g) but triples in weight when cooked
Rajma has a low glycaemic index (roughly 25–29), making it a slow-digesting carbohydrate source that supports satiety
Turning rajma into a curry barely changes the protein — the calorie increase comes almost entirely from cooking oil, similar to other Indian legume curries
A standard bowl of rajma chawal (curry + rice) delivers about 13–15g protein and 400–440 kcal, with rice contributing roughly half the calories
Add a side of curd or a small portion of paneer to push a rajma chawal meal well past 20g protein without changing the core dish
